#### ! Scenario

*Or what to do when you need to swap one library for another*
This scenario demonstrates how to replace one dependency with another in Maven. Maven has no substitution mechanism; an exclusion plus an explicit declaration of the replacement achieves the same result, one path at a time. Here `lib-a` depends on `lib-b`, which we treat as abandoned, and `lib-d` stands in as its maintained drop-in replacement.

::: {.callout-note title="Tool Versions"}
This scenario was tested with **Maven 3.9**; the behaviour shown applies to Maven 3.x.
:::

#### ! Example

```{mermaid}
%%| fig-width: 4.4
graph LR
    Root[Project Root] --> LibA[lib-a:1.0.0]
    LibA -. excluded .-> LibB["lib-b:1.0.0 (abandoned)"]
    Root --> LibD["lib-d:1.0.0 (replacement)"]
```

```{.xml include="pom.xml" snippet="s15-deps"}
```

#### ! Expect
One rule says "wherever `lib-b` appears, use `lib-d` instead", and the whole graph follows it.

#### ! Actual
There is no such rule. The tree shows `lib-a` with no children and `lib-d` beside it: the exclusion cut `lib-b` (and the `lib-c` beneath it) off *this* path, and the direct declaration supplied the replacement. A second dependency that also pulls in `lib-b` would bring it straight back.

#### ! Why
Exclusions are declaration-scoped, so a substitution in Maven is a manual composition: exclude the old artifact on every path that carries it, declare the new one once, and keep the two in step by hand. Gradle's `dependencySubstitution` expresses the same intent as one graph-wide rule ([GS15](../../gradle-demo/scenario-15-substitution/guide.qmd)). Note also that nothing checks the replacement actually provides the classes the excluded library did; that is a runtime discovery.

#### ! Fix

```{.xml include="pom.xml" snippet="s15-guard"}
```

*   **Exclude on every path:** add an `<exclusion>` to each direct dependency that transitively carries the old library.
*   **Declare the replacement once**, at the version that matches the API the excluded library's consumers expect.
*   **Guard it:** a `bannedDependencies` rule for the old coordinates (shown above) fails the build the day a new dependency smuggles it back ([MS18](../scenario-18-banning/guide.qmd)).
*   **For package-namespace migrations** (`javax.*` to `jakarta.*`), use the [Eclipse Transformer](https://github.com/eclipse-transformer/transformer) Maven plugin, which rewrites bytecode and resources at build time. The Shade plugin's relocation can do it too, but [breaks transitive dependencies and IDE debugging](https://tomee.apache.org/javax-to-jakarta.html).

#### ! Risk
* LOW Replacing a library with a drop-in that keeps the same packages and API (a logging bridge, a maintained fork).
* MEDIUM Replacing a library with a fork whose API has started to diverge; the compiler will not warn you about the transitives that call it.
* HIGH Replacing a library with something that is not a drop-in at all. Expect `NoClassDefFoundError` or `NoSuchMethodError` at runtime.

#### ! Control
*   Pair every substitution with an enforcer ban on the old coordinates.
*   Comment each exclusion with what replaces it and why.
*   Run `mvn dependency:tree` after every change and confirm the old library is absent from the *whole* tree, not just one subtree.

#### ! Check
**Fast check:** `mvn validate`, then `mvn dependency:tree`

**What to look for:** `validate` succeeds (the ban finds nothing); the tree shows `lib-d:jar:1.0.0` and no `lib-b` anywhere. Remove the `<exclusion>` and `validate` fails naming `lib-b`.

**Conclusion:** Substitution in Maven is exclusion plus declaration plus a guard; the tree is the only proof it worked.

#### ! Scales
The logging-framework swap (`log4j` → SLF4J + Logback via `log4j-over-slf4j`) is the canonical example, but the pattern applies to any migration: `javax.*` to `jakarta.*`, a community library to an internal fork, an abandoned library to a maintained alternative. In large multi-module builds the per-path exclusions become a maintenance burden; teams centralise them in the parent POM and lean on the enforcer ban to catch what the exclusions miss.

#### ! Takeaway
Maven has no graph-wide substitution. Exclude the old library on each path, declare the replacement, and guard with the Enforcer Plugin so it cannot return unnoticed.

#### ! Wild

Large enterprise projects migrating from `javax.servlet` to `jakarta.servlet` often face hundreds of modules that cannot be updated simultaneously. The [Eclipse Transformer](https://github.com/eclipse-transformer/transformer) was created specifically for this problem: it rewrites bytecode and resources to map `javax.*` to `jakarta.*` without requiring source changes. Apache TomEE [initially tried the Maven Shade Plugin's relocation feature](https://tomee.apache.org/javax-to-jakarta.html) for this purpose but abandoned it due to broken transitive dependencies and lost source and javadoc mappings. The Transformer's Maven plugin hooks into the standard build lifecycle, allowing teams to migrate one module at a time while the rest of the application continues to use the old namespace.
